title: How Terraform builds a plan
summary: Configuration, state and the real world compared.

steps.n: Terraform loads all configuration files in the folder and the modules that they call, and builds a graph of resources.
State is Terraform's record of what it manages: the real IDs and the last known attributes.
The provider reads the real objects. If someone changed a resource by hand, Terraform notices the drift here.
For each resource it decides: create, update in place, replace or destroy, or no change.
The plan lists every action with the attribute that causes it. Arguments marked "forces replacement" need special care.

steps.l: apply: call the provider in order
steps.n: Dependencies decide the order. Independent resources are created in parallel.
After each successful change the state is updated, so an interrupted apply can continue from where it stopped.

title: Detecting and fixing drift
summary: Someone changed production by hand.

steps.l: Open port 22 to the world in the console
steps.n: During an incident someone changes a security group by hand. The code and the state are not updated.
A nightly terraform plan compares the real security group with the code.
The plan wants to remove the rule. This difference between code and reality is drift.
If the change was right, update the code. If it was a shortcut, let Terraform put it back. Do not apply blindly.
Applying removes the manual rule. For a new resource created by hand, terraform import brings it under management.
Give read-only access to most people, and use break-glass roles that are logged.

steps.l: Alert on drift in a pipeline
steps.n: A scheduled plan that fails when it finds changes turns drift into a ticket, instead of a surprise.

title: Public and private subnets, NAT and the internet
summary: Which route table sends traffic where.

steps.l: App needs to call an update server
steps.n: The server in the private subnet has only a private address. Nobody on the internet can start a connection to it.
The private subnet route table sends all non-local traffic to the NAT gateway.
The NAT gateway replaces the private source address with its own public address and remembers the connection.

steps.l: Public subnet route: 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW
steps.n: The route table of the public subnet points to the internet gateway, which connects the VPC to the internet.
The internet service sees the public address of the NAT gateway only.
The reply comes back to the NAT gateway, which maps it to the original private address.
Outbound works but inbound does not start here. NAT gateways charge by hour and by data, and a VPC endpoint avoids them for cloud services.

title: Multi-window burn rate alerting
summary: Page fast for big problems, ticket slowly for small ones.

steps.n: The budget is the share of requests that may fail in the SLO period. Burn rate says how fast it is being spent.

steps.l: Burn rate 14.4 for the last hour
steps.n: At this speed 2 percent of the monthly budget is gone in one hour. The whole budget would be gone in about two days.
A short window confirms that the problem is still happening, so the page stops soon after the fix.
A fast burn needs a human now. The page links to a runbook and the dashboard.
A slower burn does not need a night call, but it will empty the budget before the month ends.

steps.l: Open a ticket for the daytime
steps.n: A ticket is picked up during working hours. This keeps pages for what is urgent and avoids alert fatigue.
Review thresholds after incidents and false alarms. Alerts should match the SLO, not every cause of trouble.

title: Running a chaos experiment safely
summary: Hypothesis, small blast radius, abort rule.

steps.n: For example: if one of three replicas dies, the success rate stays above 99.9 percent.

steps.l: Define steady state and abort rule
steps.n: Pick the metrics that show health, and say in advance when to stop, such as errors above 1 percent for two minutes.

steps.l: Announce and limit the blast radius
steps.n: Tell the on-call team. Start in staging, or with one pod or a small share of traffic in production.

steps.l: Inject the fault: kill a pod
steps.n: The tool injects one fault at a time, such as killing a pod, adding latency or blocking a dependency.
Someone watches the steady-state metrics during the whole run and keeps a finger on the stop button.
The experiment ends after the planned time, or earlier if the abort rule is hit. All changes are reverted.

steps.l: Record the result and fix the gap
steps.n: If the hypothesis failed, you found a weakness cheaply. Make an action with an owner and repeat the test after the fix.

title: An HTTPS request through a Kubernetes ingress
summary: Load balancer, ingress controller, Service and pod.

steps.n: DNS maps the name to the public address of the cloud load balancer.
The load balancer sends traffic to the nodes where the ingress controller pods run.

steps.l: Terminate TLS, match host and path
steps.n: The controller uses the certificate from a Secret and matches the host and the path against Ingress rules.
The rule for /api points to the Service named api. A wrong service name or port gives a 503.
The Service sends the request to a pod that passes its readiness probe.
The answer returns along the same path. Each hop adds a little latency and has its own timeout.

steps.l: Where to look when it fails
steps.n: A 404 means no rule matched. A 502 or 503 means no healthy backend. Check kubectl describe ingress and the controller logs.

title: How a TCP connection closes, and TIME_WAIT
summary: FIN, ACK and why sockets stay for a while.

steps.l: FIN: I have no more to send
steps.n: The side that finishes first sends a FIN segment. This closes one direction of the connection.
The other side acknowledges. It can still send data, which is called a half-closed connection.

steps.l: FIN: I am done as well
steps.n: When the server has no more data, it sends its own FIN.
The client acknowledges the last FIN, so both sides know that the connection has ended.
The side that closed first keeps the socket for about 60 seconds, so late packets from the old connection cannot confuse a new one.
The server frees its socket as soon as it sees the last ACK. Many TIME_WAIT sockets on a busy client are normal.
If you run out of ports, use keep-alive and connection pools instead of tuning the kernel. Check with ss -s.

title: How the OOM killer picks a victim
summary: Memory pressure, reclaim and the kill.

steps.n: A service grows, for example from a leak or a traffic spike. The kernel gives pages when they are touched.
First the kernel frees page cache, which is cheap. It may also swap out cold pages, which is slow.
When free memory and swap run out, the kernel cannot satisfy an allocation. Waiting longer will not help.
The OOM killer scores each process by memory use and adjustments, and chooses the one that frees the most memory with the least harm.
The chosen process is killed at once with no cleanup. It is often your biggest service, not the one that leaked.
Look for "Out of memory: Killed process" in dmesg -T or journalctl -k. In containers the cgroup limit gives exit code 137.
Set memory limits per service, alert on available memory, and find the leak. Adding swap hides a problem, it does not solve it.

title: How a device gets an IP address with DHCP
summary: Discover, offer, request, acknowledge, and what happens when the lease runs out.

steps.n: A device that joins the network has no IP address, so it can only send broadcasts on the local segment.
The device asks everybody on the segment: is there a DHCP server? It uses 0.0.0.0 as its source address.
The server picks a free address from its pool and offers it, with a lease time, a mask, a gateway and DNS servers.
The device accepts one offer. It is still a broadcast, so that other servers learn their offers were not used.
The server records the lease and confirms. The device can now configure its interface with the address and the gateway.
The device starts to use the network. If another device already used that address, you would see a conflict, so servers check the pool carefully.
After half of the lease time the device asks the same server to extend the lease, so its address does not change while it stays online.
The server extends the lease. If the server is unreachable, the device tries again later, and after the lease ends it must start from DISCOVER.

title: How a CDN serves a cached page
summary: Edge cache hit, cache miss, and why headers decide what is stored.

steps.n: The browser is sent to the nearest edge location, usually by DNS or anycast routing, and asks for the file.
The edge builds a cache key from the URL, and some headers, and checks whether it holds a fresh copy.
The edge does not have the object, so it makes a request to the origin server. Only this first request travels the long way.
The origin replies with the file and headers. Cache-Control says how long the copy may be reused.
The edge stores the object and returns it. The first visitor sees the slower path.
Another user in the same region asks for the same file a minute later.
The edge answers from its cache with no trip to the origin. This lowers latency and the load on the origin.
When the copy is stale, the edge can ask the origin if it changed, using ETag. A 304 means the stored copy is still good.

title: Cleaning up with trap when a script is stopped
summary: How trap runs your cleanup on exit, on Ctrl+C and on errors.

steps.n: The script registers a function to run when the shell exits or receives an interrupt or terminate signal.
The script creates a temporary directory for its work. It is the thing that must be removed at the end.
The script downloads and processes files in the temporary directory. This may take minutes.
The terminal sends SIGINT to the script. Without a trap the script would stop and leave the directory behind.
Bash calls the registered function before it ends. The function removes the temporary directory and releases locks.
The cleanup removes files with a quoted variable. If the variable were empty, an unquoted command could delete the wrong path, so check it first.
The shell exits with the proper status code. A SIGKILL cannot be trapped, so cleanup may not run in that case.

title: Automatic rollback after a failed health check
summary: A deploy that watches its own health and returns to the last good version.

steps.n: The pipeline asks the orchestrator to roll out the new version, and remembers that version 41 was the last good one.
The orchestrator starts a small share of instances on version 42 and keeps the rest on version 41.
Monitoring compares the new instances with the old ones over a set time window, using the same signals your SLO uses.
The new version is clearly worse than the baseline. This is a failed check, and it does not need a person to notice it.
The pipeline tells the orchestrator to restore the last good version and stops the rollout.
The new instances are drained and removed. Users on the old instances were never affected much, because the exposure was small.
The pipeline marks the change as failed, notifies the owner and links the data. Later, the team fixes the cause and tries again.

title: How a private server reaches the internet through NAT
summary: Route table, NAT gateway, and why the internet cannot start connections back.

steps.n: The server has only a private address such as 10.0.2.15, so the internet cannot route replies to it directly.
The route table of the private subnet sends all non-local traffic to the NAT gateway in a public subnet.
The gateway replaces the private source with its own public address and records the mapping for this connection.
The internet host sees only the gateway address. The host does not know the private address of the server.
The reply returns to the public address of the gateway, as for any other client.
The gateway finds the mapping, restores the private destination, and forwards the reply to the server.
A host that tries to connect to the private server first has no mapping, so the gateway drops it. This is why NAT hides the server.
NAT gateways bill by the amount of data processed, so large downloads can cost much. Use endpoints for cloud storage and registries.

title: How a pre-signed URL gives temporary access
summary: Letting a user upload to a private bucket without sharing credentials.

steps.n: The user asks the application for permission to upload. The bucket itself stays private.
The application authenticates the user and decides whether this upload is allowed, and for which path.
Using its own credentials, the application creates a signature for one object key, one method and a short expiry, for example 5 minutes.
The URL contains the signature in its query string. Anybody who holds it can use it until it expires, so treat it like a password.

steps.l: PUT the file to the URL
steps.n: The browser sends the file directly to storage. The data does not pass through the application server.
Storage recomputes the signature and checks the expiry and the permissions of the signer. The request is accepted only if everything matches.
The object is stored. After the expiry time the same URL stops working.

title: How docker pull downloads only the layers it needs
summary: Manifest, layers, the local cache, and why base images matter.

steps.n: The CLI sends the request to the daemon, which does the work.

steps.l: Ask for the manifest of the tag
steps.n: The daemon asks the registry for the manifest. It lists the layers of the image by digest and the configuration.
The registry returns the list. Each layer is identified by a hash of its content, so the same layer has the same ID everywhere.
The daemon checks which layer digests are already on disk. Layers from the same base image are likely to be present.
Only the two new layers are downloaded, in parallel. Three layers say Already exists.
Each layer is checked against its digest, and then unpacked into the storage driver.
The image is ready. A tag can move, so for production deployments use the digest, which never changes.

title: Readiness probes and traffic
summary: How a pod is added to and removed from a Service without dropping requests.

steps.n: The application starts, loads its cache and connects to the database. This takes about 20 seconds.
The kubelet calls the probe on the schedule given in the spec. A failure or timeout means not ready.
The pod answers that it is still starting. It is not in the list of endpoints, so no traffic is sent to it.
The kubelet keeps asking. Meanwhile the old pods carry the load.
The application has finished starting and the probe succeeds as many times as the success threshold requires.

steps.l: Add the pod to the endpoints
steps.n: The pod IP is added to the endpoint list of the Service, and the proxies on every node update their rules.
Traffic is spread across all ready pods. If the probe later fails, the pod is removed from the list again, without a restart.

title: How systemd restarts a crashing service
summary: Restart policy, back-off, and the start limit that stops a restart loop.

steps.n: systemd runs the command from the unit file. With Restart=on-failure it will react to a non-zero exit.
Standard output and errors of the process are captured by the journal, so you can read them with journalctl -u name.
The process crashes, for example because of a missing config file. systemd sees the exit status.
systemd waits for the configured time before trying again, for example 5 seconds, to avoid a busy loop.
The service is started again. If the cause is not fixed it fails again. This repeats.
After StartLimitBurst failures within StartLimitIntervalSec, systemd stops trying and marks the unit as failed.
An operator runs journalctl, fixes the config, and then uses systemctl reset-failed before starting the service again.

title: How Prometheus scrapes and stores metrics
summary: Targets, scrape, storage, query, and why the pull model helps.

steps.n: Prometheus knows what to scrape from static config or service discovery, for example from Kubernetes pods.
Prometheus pulls the current values in a text format. The application only needs to expose them.
The reply lists metric names with labels and values, such as http_requests_total{status="500"} 42.
Each series gets a new sample. Storage cost grows with the number of series, so labels must have few values.
A successful scrape also sets the up metric, and a failed one sets it to 0. That is how you notice a dead target.
Grafana sends a PromQL query. rate turns an ever-growing counter into a per-second value.
The result is drawn as a graph. Alert rules use the same queries and fire when a condition holds for a given time.

title: Why every HTTP call needs a timeout
summary: What happens to a script when the server stops answering.

steps.n: The script makes a call with no timeout argument. By default the library waits with no limit.
The library connects and sends the request over the network.
The server accepts the connection and then stops responding, for example because it is overloaded or a firewall dropped packets.
With no timeout the call never returns. The script stays stuck, and a cron job or worker slot is used up for good.
The fix: 3 seconds to connect and 10 seconds to read. The numbers are chosen from what is normal for the service.
After the limit the library raises an exception. The script can retry with back-off, or report a failure.
The script logs the problem with the URL and the time, and moves on or exits with an error. It does not hang.

title: How an alert escalates to a person
summary: Page, acknowledge, escalate and hand over to an incident commander.

steps.n: Monitoring decides that users are affected and creates a page, with a link to the runbook and the dashboard.
The paging system calls the primary on-call engineer with a push, a text and a phone call.
The engineer acknowledges within the target time. This stops the escalation timer, and tells others someone is on it.
The engineer looks at the dashboard and the latest deploy. A rollback might be the fastest mitigation.
The problem is larger than expected, so the engineer pages the secondary, who joins the call.
Impact is large, so the incident commander takes over coordination, while the engineers continue the technical work.
The commander posts status updates on a schedule and writes down decisions. This is the raw material for the postmortem.
Without an acknowledgement, the system escalates to the secondary after a set time, then to a manager. This is why escalation policies matter.

title: Bringing an existing resource under Terraform with import
summary: Config first, import into state, then plan until there is no diff.

steps.l: A bucket exists but is not managed
steps.n: Someone created it in the console. Terraform does not know about it, and a plan would try to create a second one.
The engineer writes configuration for the bucket with its real name. An import block or the import command connects the two.
During import, Terraform asks the cloud API for the attributes of the existing bucket.
The resource is added to the state under its address. Nothing in the cloud has changed yet.
The plan compares the configuration with the state. Differences show where the code does not match the real settings.
For example, the tags in the code are missing in reality. The engineer adjusts the code until the plan shows no changes.
Only when the plan is clean or shows changes you want do you apply. From now on, changes go through code.

title: How an app gets a secret without storing it
summary: Workload identity, a secrets manager and a short-lived credential.

steps.l: Start up with no secret inside
steps.n: The container image holds no passwords. It only knows where to ask and which identity it runs as.
The platform gives the pod or function a signed identity token. The app presents it to the identity service.
The identity service verifies the signature, the issuer and the audience, and maps the workload to a role.
The service returns temporary credentials that expire in about an hour. Nothing long-lived is stored on disk.
The app asks the secrets manager for one secret, using the temporary credentials.
The manager checks that this role may read only this secret, then writes an audit record of who read it and when.
The app keeps the value in memory and connects to the database. A rotation job changes the secret on a schedule.

title: Security gates in a pull request
summary: Scans that run before code can merge.

steps.n: The developer pushes a branch and opens a pull request, which triggers the pipeline on a clean, isolated runner.
A scanner reads the diff and the history of the branch for keys and tokens. A match stops the pipeline at once.
Software composition analysis lists known vulnerabilities in libraries. Static analysis flags unsafe code patterns.
Infrastructure checks find open firewalls. The image scan reports packages with known fixes.
Results are summarised in the pull request. The policy fails the build for high findings that have a fix.
The developer updates the library, pushes again and the scans repeat. Small fixes are cheap at this stage.
A reviewer sees green checks, reads the change and approves. The branch rules block merge without both.

title: Signing an image and verifying it at deploy time
summary: From build to a cluster that only runs trusted images.

steps.n: The pipeline builds on a clean runner from pinned inputs and records an SBOM.
The registry stores the image and returns its digest, a hash of the content that cannot change.
The pipeline asks the signing service to sign the digest with a key or an identity bound token. The signature is stored next to the image.
Later, someone applies a deployment. The admission controller looks up the image reference before the pod is created.
The controller checks that the signature is valid and was made by the expected pipeline identity.
A valid signature lets the pod start. An unsigned or altered image is rejected with a clear message.
The deny event reaches the team. This is how a tampered or untested image is stopped before it runs.

title: How a default deny network policy works
summary: Blocking all pod traffic, then allowing only what is needed.

steps.n: Before any policy exists, every pod can reach every other pod. This is what an attacker relies on after a breach.
A policy that selects all pods and lists no allowed ingress is applied. The plugin programs rules on every node.
The web pod connects directly to the database. The plugin drops the packet because no rule allows it.
The team adds a policy: the API pod may reach the database on port 5432. Everything else stays blocked.
The plugin matches the labels of the source and port. The connection is allowed and works as before.
A second allow rule permits web to API on port 8080. The path the application needs is open.
A compromised web pod can now reach only one port on one service, which limits what an attacker can do.

title: The first hour of a security incident
summary: Detect, contain, preserve evidence and start recovery.

steps.l: Alert: shell in a production container
steps.n: A runtime detection fires. It names the pod, the user and the command that started.
The on-call checks the deploy log and the audit trail. Nobody has a reason to be in that container.
The on-call pages the incident commander, who opens a channel, assigns roles and starts a timeline.
The commander has the pod isolated with a deny network policy, and the service account token revoked. Pods are not deleted yet.
A snapshot of the volume and the pod logs are copied to a protected location for the investigation.
Secrets the pod could read are rotated. The workload is redeployed from a known good, signed image.
Stakeholders get updates on a schedule. Afterward the team holds a blameless review and ships the control changes.

title: How exit codes and pipefail decide success
summary: Why a failed step inside a pipe can go unnoticed.

steps.n: The shell starts both commands, with the output of A connected to the input of B.
The first command hits an error, for example a missing file, and exits with status 2.
B receives no data, finishes normally and exits with status 0.
Without pipefail the pipeline reports the status of the last command only, so the failure of A is hidden.
With pipefail the pipeline returns the status of the last command that failed, which is 2.
Now the script exits at that line instead of going on with bad data. Use it together with checks of results that matter.

title: Switching traffic with a blue-green deploy
summary: Two identical environments and a fast, safe switch.

steps.n: The current version runs in the blue environment and receives all traffic.

steps.l: Deploy the new version to green
steps.n: The pipeline installs the new version in an identical idle environment. Users do not see it.
Automated checks call the green environment directly. Caches are warmed so the first users do not see slow pages.
One configuration change sends new requests to green. Existing connections finish on blue.
Error rate and latency on green are compared with the blue baseline for several minutes.
Rollback is the same single switch in the other direction. Blue is still running and untouched.
After a safe period, blue is kept as the next idle environment. Database changes must work for both versions.

title: Reaching cloud storage privately with an endpoint
summary: Keeping traffic off the internet and off the NAT gateway.

steps.n: The application uses the storage API name. DNS resolves it to a private address when an endpoint exists.
The route table has an entry that sends the storage prefix to the endpoint, not to the NAT gateway.
The packet goes through the provider network inside your virtual network. It never touches the public internet.
The service receives the request and sees that it comes from the endpoint of your network.
A policy on the endpoint and one on the bucket both allow only your account. A request for another account bucket is denied.
The data comes back through the endpoint. There is no NAT data charge and no public path to monitor.

title: How a container health check works
summary: From a probe command to a restart decision.

steps.n: The process starts and needs a few seconds before it can serve requests.
At each interval the daemon runs the command from HEALTHCHECK inside the container, for example a request to /health.
The command fails because the app is not ready. The status is starting during the start period, then counts failures.
After the set number of failures in a row the status changes to unhealthy.
The status is visible in docker ps and to the orchestrator, which can stop sending traffic to it.
The orchestrator or a restart policy replaces the unhealthy container. The cause should still be found in the logs.

title: How a ConfigMap change reaches a pod
summary: Env vars versus mounted files and why pods need a restart sometimes.

steps.n: The engineer applies a changed ConfigMap. The API server stores the new version in etcd.
The kubelet on each node watches the objects used by its pods and sees the update.
For a ConfigMap mounted as files, the kubelet refreshes the files after a short delay. A program that reads them again sees the new values.
Values copied into environment variables at start-up do not change. The process keeps what it was given.
To apply env changes, the engineer restarts the rollout, or uses a checksum annotation so a change triggers a new revision.

steps.l: New pods start with new values
steps.n: Pods are replaced gradually, each reading the current ConfigMap, with readiness checks protecting traffic.

title: How the kernel chooses which process to kill
summary: Out of memory, OOM scores and what you can do about it.

steps.n: A service keeps allocating memory. The kernel agrees as long as free memory or swap exists.
No free pages are left and reclaiming cache does not help. The kernel must free memory or stop.
The kernel gives each process a badness score based on memory use, adjusted by oom_score_adj.
The process with the highest score receives SIGKILL. It has no chance to log or clean up.
The kernel logs the victim and the memory state. The administrator finds it with dmesg or the journal.
Set limits with cgroups, fix the leak, add memory or protect key services with a lower oom_score_adj.

title: HTTP to HTTPS and HSTS
summary: Why the first request is the weak one.

steps.n: The user types the name without a scheme, so the browser tries plain HTTP first.
The server redirects to HTTPS. This first request travelled unencrypted and could be altered by someone on the path.
The browser connects with TLS and verifies the certificate before sending the request.
The response says: always use HTTPS for this name for the next year, including subdomains if you choose.
The browser stores the HSTS policy. Later visits skip the plain HTTP step completely.
Sites can join a preload list built into browsers, so even the very first visit is protected.

title: From an alert to the cause
summary: How metrics, traces and logs work together in an investigation.

steps.n: The alert fires on a symptom: 6 percent of requests fail. It links to a dashboard and a runbook.
The graph shows errors began at 14:05, right after a deployment marker. One service stands out.
A trace of one failed request shows the time spent. The call to the payment service takes 30 seconds then fails.
Logs from the payment service for that trace show connection pool exhausted. The cause is clear.
The engineer rolls back the 14:00 release. The error rate returns to normal within minutes.
Notes from the alert, graphs and log lines go into the incident record for the review.

title: How a with block cleans up
summary: Files and locks that are closed even when errors occur.

steps.n: The with statement calls the object enter method. For a file this opens it and returns the file object.
Your block runs using f. The operating system holds a file descriptor until it is released.
Midway through the block an error occurs, such as a parse failure on a bad line.
Python calls the exit method before the exception continues. The file is closed.
The error is passed to the caller or handler, with no leaked file descriptor left behind.

steps.l: Same idea for locks and connections
steps.n: Any object with enter and exit works, and contextlib helps you write your own for temporary directories or timers.

title: The weekly reliability review
summary: Using the error budget to decide what to do next.

steps.n: The review starts with the facts: current availability, budget left and the burn rate of the past week.
At day 20 of 28, more than half of the budget is spent, and most of it by one incident.
The group looks at the incident review. Two action items are still open, one of them a missing alert.
The product team lists releases planned for the next week. One touches the same component.
The error budget policy says: slow risky releases and finish reliability work first when more than half is gone.
The decisions and owners are written down, and the next review checks them. The numbers, not opinions, set the pace.

title: Reading a plan before you apply
summary: Spotting replacements and surprises.

steps.n: Terraform reads the state and the real resources, then computes the difference to the code.

steps.l: Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy
steps.n: The summary is the first thing to read. A destroy that you did not expect is a stop sign.
Lines marked forces replacement mean the old resource is deleted and a new one created, which may lose data.

steps.l: Share the plan in the pull request
steps.n: The reviewer reads the plan output rather than only the code, and checks names, counts and sensitive changes.

steps.l: Approve or ask for a change
steps.n: If the plan shows a surprise, the code changes and a new plan is created. Nothing has been applied yet.
Applying the saved plan guarantees that what was reviewed is exactly what runs.

title: How zero trust checks one request
summary: Identity, device and policy are checked every time.

steps.n: The user opens an internal app from a managed laptop. The request goes to the proxy, not straight to the app.
The proxy verifies the sign-in with a hardware key, the device health, and the session age.
A central policy says which groups may reach this app and from which device state. A failure stops the request here.
The proxy passes a signed token that names the user and expires in minutes.
The application checks that this user may read this record. The proxy check alone is not enough.

steps.l: Return the data and log the decision
steps.n: Every allow and deny is logged, so an investigator can reconstruct who reached what.

title: Sign in with OIDC and call an API
summary: From login to an access token and a protected call.

steps.n: The app sends the user to the identity provider with its client id, scope and a random state value.
The user signs in with a passkey. The provider never gives the password to the app.
The provider redirects back with a one-time authorization code.
The app swaps the code, with a proof key, for an ID token and a short-lived access token.

steps.l: Call the API with the token
steps.n: The access token is sent in a header, never in the URL.
The API checks signature, issuer, audience, expiry and scope before doing any work.
The response contains only what the scope and the user's permissions allow.

title: How parameterised queries stop injection
summary: The same input, treated as text instead of code.

steps.n: The attacker enters x' OR '1'='1 into a search box.
The code builds SELECT ... WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1' and sends it as text.
The condition is always true, so every row is returned.
The attacker receives all users. This is the harm of injection.
The code sends the query with a placeholder and the value separately.
The database searches for a user literally named x' OR '1'='1 and finds none.
